extracted.intended_audience: life-sciences and biotech research teams, data engineers, data scientists, R&D IT leaders, and informaticians seeking to implement FAIR data practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) in life sciences and biotech contexts, with practical actions for metadata, identifiers, formats, access, provenance, licensing and infrastructure. Targets teams building data platforms, catalogs and pipelines for multi-modal research data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findable (FAIR principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data should be easy for researchers and computer systems to discover. This means assigning globally unique and persistent identifiers (such as DOIs or UUIDs) to all datasets and ensuring datasets are indexed with rich, machine-actionable metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findability 'lays the groundwork for efficient knowledge reuse' by making research data, assays, and results easy to locate across departments, collaborators, and platforms. Examples: assign persistent identifiers and index datasets in searchable catalogs. Anti-patterns: datasets without persistent IDs or minimal/no metadata that cannot be discovered by computational systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign persistent identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign persistent identifiers such as DOIs (Digital Object Identifiers) for published datasets or UUIDs for internal records to ensure long-term traceability for all data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent IDs provide global uniqueness and persistence so datasets remain findable over time. Use DOIs for public releases and UUIDs for internal assets. Ensure the identifier is machine-actionable and attached to the dataset's metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create centralized and searchable data catalogs
rubrics_metrics.description: Build centralized catalogs that facilitate search so users across departments can locate datasets based on key attributes, context or modality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized catalogs reduce fragmentation and duplication by making it easy to search for datasets. Catalogs should expose machine-readable metadata and support attribute-based queries. Example: unify datasets from diverse sources into a searchable index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized metadata schemas (Findable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standardized metadata schemas such as ISA-Tab, Dublin Core or MIAME to describe datasets in a machine-readable and domain-relevant way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich, machine-actionable metadata is essential for discoverability and downstream AI/ML. Adopt domain-appropriate schemas and ensure metadata is consistent across datasets. Anti-patterns: ad-hoc or inconsistent metadata and free-text descriptions with no schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible (FAIR principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data must be retrievable by users through standardized communication protocols, even if the data is restricted; restricted data should have clear permissions and metadata describing how to request access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility focuses on implementing infrastructure that supports controlled data access at scale (APIs, authenticated endpoints). Even when data is not open, provide machine-actionable metadata that explains access procedures. Anti-patterns: secure data with no documented access path or no metadata describing access rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define access protocols and permissions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparently communicate which users and systems can access what data and under what conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and publish access/control policies in machine-readable ways where possible. Include authorization and authentication mechanisms, roles, and conditions for data use. Example: clearly documented permissions and processes to request access for restricted datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store data in environments with APIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Store data in environments with APIs or governed interfaces (such as S3 buckets, FAIR Data Points or cloud-based research platforms) to allow secure access at scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: APIs and governed interfaces enable programmatic, auditable access and prevent ad-hoc file-sharing. Avoid burying data in unsearchable file shares or scanned PDFs without programmatic access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure restricted datasets include rich metadata about access
rubrics_metrics.description: Even restricted datasets should include rich metadata that describes the data and how a user can request or gain access through appropriate channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metadata for restricted data should specify permissions, contact points, consent/usage constraints and the process to obtain access. Anti-patterns: restricted data with metadata that only says 'restricted' and gives no further instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperable (FAIR principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data needs to be machine-readable and compatible with other systems and formats outside of the initial experimental environment; described using standardized vocabularies and ontologies and stored in machine-readable formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interoperability enables integration across multi-modal datasets (genomics, imaging, clinical). It requires semantic consistency (ontologies), appropriate formats, and machine-actionable encodings rather than free text or PDFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized data formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use domain-appropriate, standardized data formats such as VCF for genomic variants, HDF5 for high-dimensional bioimaging or JSON for structured clinical records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing well-known formats promotes tool compatibility and reduces conversion overhead. Anti-patterns: storing critical research data only in CSVs, PDFs, or bespoke binary blobs without standardized schemas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt shared ontologies and controlled vocabularies
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt shared ontologies and controlled vocabularies like those from the OBO Foundry, CDISC, or SNOMED CT to ensure semantic consistency across projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community vocabularies to avoid semantic mismatches. Document which ontology terms are used and map local codes to standard terminologies. Example: map gene/disease names to established vocabularies to enable cross-study integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize for machine-actionability
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode relationships, metadata and variables in structured, parsable formats rather than in free text or PDFs so computational systems and AI can understand and read the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor structured representations (JSON, RDF, typed fields) and avoid burying metadata in human-readable but machine-unfriendly formats. Ensure metadata and data encodings are consistent and explicitly typed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusable (FAIR principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data must be able to be easily replicated and studied in new contexts; requires clarity on licensing and usage rights, robust documentation of provenance, quality and context, and rich metadata annotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusability maximizes dataset utility by providing provenance, quality metrics, licensing and contextual documentation so others can trust and repurpose the data. Anti-patterns: data without provenance, missing transformation logs, or unclear licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply clear licensing terms and citation guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply clear licensing terms (e.g., CC-BY and CC0) and citation guidelines to enable reuse with appropriate attribution and legal certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make licensing machine-readable where possible. Document permitted uses, attribution requirements, and any restrictions (privacy, IP). Lack of licensing inhibits confident reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rich metadata capturing provenance and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach metadata that captures the who, what, when and how of the dataset, including instruments used, conditions, access restrictions, transformations and assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance and context information help researchers evaluate fitness-for-purpose. Capture processing steps, pipelines, parameter settings and original data sources. Anti-patterns: releasing derived data without provenance or transformation history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate and document data quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate and document data quality with logs, QA metrics or provenance records so users can trust and verify findings using your documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include QA checks, validation reports, and known limitations. Provide machine-readable QA metrics where possible. Example: maintain logs and QC metrics to support reproducibility and regulatory review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support multi-modal data with scalable infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use data infrastructure that can manage high-dimensional and large-volume files (genomics, imaging, single-cell, spatial omics) rather than platforms built only for tabular data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infrastructure must handle diverse modalities, large files, and performance needs; otherwise organizations resort to workarounds that fragment data. Anti-patterns: relying solely on relational/tabular platforms that cannot scale for high-resolution imaging or sequence data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address fragmented data systems and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Unify siloed data environments and harmonize formats so datasets from different teams and systems can be indexed, queried and shared efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and remediate fragmentation by centralizing catalogs, standardizing formats/metadata, and reducing duplicated storage and incompatible systems. Example: consolidation of imaging, genomics and clinical data into interoperable catalogs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational readiness and FAIR-awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement change management to overcome cultural resistance; secure leadership buy-in and educate researchers, informaticians and engineers on FAIR benefits and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAIR is as much a people/process problem as a technical one. Create incentives, training and governance to shift from isolated data ownership to shared, reusable assets. Anti-patterns: treating FAIR as purely administrative overhead with no visible scientific benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance, consent-tracking and auditable access
rubrics_metrics.description: Track provenance and consent (e.g., consent-tracking systems, access logs and audit trails) so restricted data is traceable and compliant with ethical/regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement consent and audit mechanisms (logs, statuses, resource consumption) and ensure provenance records are attached to data. Example: consent-tracking integrated into a data mesh to manage diagnostic/genomic datasets; anti-patterns include lack of auditability for restricted human-subject data.
